t: Count Items Matching a Rule with One Linear Pass
o: Every item is a triple (type, color, name), and the rule selects items whose field named by ruleKey equals ruleValue; we just count them. In example 1 exactly one item is silver. Example 2 counts items typed "phone" and deliberately includes a computer whose NAME is "phone" to stress that only the keyed field participates. With up to 10^4 items and three fixed positions, one linear pass comparing strings is already optimal - no preprocessing or extra structure can beat it.
k: Only the field addressed by ruleKey matters - other fields coincidentally equal to ruleValue are ignored.
Mapping ruleKey to a column index (type->0, color->1, name->2) turns the rule into a plain equality test.
A single scan is asymptotically optimal; the only decision is code clarity.

a.i: Check each item against the rule verbatim: depending on ruleKey, compare the corresponding destructured field with ruleValue. This mirrors the statement one-to-one and needs no lookup table.
s: For each item, extract type, color, name.
If the ruleKey-specific field equals ruleValue, increment the counter.
a.t: O(n*L) - each of n items compares strings of length up to L = 10

a.n: Approach 2: Rule Key to Index Mapping
a.i: Translate ruleKey once into the column index it designates, then every loop iteration collapses to a single indexed comparison. This hoists the three-way branch out of the hot loop and reads cleanly with filter/count idioms.
s: Scan items and compare item[idx] with ruleValue.
a.t: O(n*L) - same comparisons with the key branch hoisted out of the loop

w: Either approach passes; prefer the index-map version for clarity. Pitfalls: comparing the wrong column (example 2 hides a decoy whose name equals the searched type value) and case sensitivity (everything is lowercase here, so direct equality is fine). Follow-ups: multiple simultaneous rules (conjunction of conditions), range-valued rules, or streaming items - the same single-pass counting pattern extends naturally.
